This leads to a quantum geometric structure of a nested fiber bundle, in which each fiber of a layer is itself a fiber bundle of the next layer. The nonadiabatic renormalization group brings a new type of tensor network states that shares physical legs among ''sites'' and encodes quantum entanglement beyond conventional matrix product states. We demonstrate how to apply the nonadiabatic renormalization group to different types of problems, including an interacting boson model and ab initio quantum chemistry with interacting electrons.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a nonadiabatic renormalization group approach to manage multiscale strong interactions in quantum systems.
AI.motivation: To tackle complex quantum systems with multiscale interactions without losing essential high-energy information.
AI.method: The method involves iteratively suppressing fast high-energy degrees of freedom using a structure resembling a nested fiber bundle, creating a new type of tensor network state that encapsulates quantum entanglement more effectively than traditional methods.
AI.result: The framework is applied successfully to various problems, demonstrating its efficacy in modeling interacting bosons and electron interactions in quantum chemistry.
AI.conclusion: The nonadiabatic renormalization group method offers a robust tool for exploring strongly correlated quantum systems, enhancing our understanding of entanglement and interactions.

title: Demonstration of Exponential Quantum Speedup with Constant-Depth Compiled Circuits for Simon's Problem
summary: We demonstrate exponential quantum speedup for a restricted-Hamming-weight version of Simon's problem on present-day superconducting quantum processors by introducing a hardware-aware compilation strategy that compiles the quantum part of each Simon query circuit to constant depth. The resulting compiled circuits have $O(1)$ depth and linear connectivity, map directly onto common device layouts, and avoid additional routing and SWAP overhead. Implemented on IBM's $156$-qubit Boston and $120$-qubit Miami processors, the resulting circuits achieve sufficiently high fidelity to exhibit algorithmic quantum speedup without error suppression. Using the number-of-queries-to-solution metric, we observe exponential speedup over the classical lower bound across the full Hamming-weight range studied on Boston and across low-to-intermediate Hamming weights on Miami; at higher Hamming weights on Miami, we still observe polynomial speedup. The same construction also reaches a regime where the original Simon problem is recovered for the problem sizes studied. These results show that careful hardware-aware compilation can make exponential quantum speedup experimentally accessible for a canonical hidden-subgroup problem in the NISQ regime.

AI.tldr: This study achieves exponential quantum speedup for a restricted version of Simon's problem on current superconducting quantum processors through an innovative compilation strategy.
AI.motivation: The research aims to demonstrate practical quantum speedup for Simon's problem using existing quantum hardware, addressing challenges in compiler design and circuit implementation.
AI.method: A hardware-aware compilation strategy was introduced to compile Simon query circuits to constant depth (O(1)) with linear connectivity, suitable for common quantum device layouts.
AI.result: Exponential speedup was observed across a broad range of Hamming weights on IBM's processors, with high fidelity enabling algorithmic quantum speedup without error suppression.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight that effective compilation techniques can facilitate significant quantum speedup for hidden-subgroup problems in Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) systems.

title: Galilean boost invariance does not survive the trace: symmetry breaking in open quantum systems
summary: Tracing out a Galilean-invariant Caldeira-Leggett environment breaks Galilean boost covariance of the reduced dynamics, while spatial translations and rotations survive intact. An operator-level analysis of the exact Hu-Paz-Zhang master equation localizes the violation entirely in the dissipative anticommutator term, scaling with the damping coefficient $Γ(t)f(t)$. The fluctuation-dissipation theorem ties this coefficient to the absorptive bath response that drives equilibrium momentum diffusion, so for any non-trivial bath spectral density bilinear-coupled Galilean invariance, the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, and reduced boost covariance cannot hold simultaneously. The stochastic decomposition of the influence functional extends the mechanism beyond the quadratic regime. The dimensionless ratio $\hbarγ/k_\mathrm{B} T$ delineates the crossover: cold atoms in dissipative optical lattices and ultracold molecules sit at its edge. Parametric driving offers a one-directional escape: the squeezing rate that protects nonequilibrium entanglement above the standard quantum limit also suppresses boost-breaking over a driving cycle.

AI.tldr: This paper examines how Galilean invariance is compromised in a Caldeira-Leggett environment, affecting the dynamics of a quantum system, particularly through the dissipative terms in the master equation, linking this violation to fluctuations in dissipative baths and suggesting that certain physical conditions may allow for recovery of boost covariance.
AI.motivation: To explore the implications of a Galilean-invariant Caldeira-Leggett environment and understand the limitations it imposes on reduced quantum dynamics and boost covariance.
AI.method: An operator-level analysis of the Hu-Paz-Zhang master equation to identify the role of dissipative terms in breaking Galilean boost covariance and a stochastic decomposition of the influence functional extending beyond the quadratic regime.
AI.result: The study reveals that any non-trivial bath interactions result in a fundamental trade-off where Galilean invariance and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem cannot simultaneously hold, establishing a framework to analyze this violation based on the damping coefficient and spectral density.
AI.conclusion: Parametric driving may restore certain symmetries by suppressing boost-breaking effects, fundamentally linking nonequilibrium entanglement properties of cold atomic systems to their environment and driving conditions.

title: Finite Imaginary-Time Evolution for Polynomial Unconstrained Binary Optimization
summary: Imaginary-time evolution is a standard primitive for ground-state preparation but is nonunitary, precluding direct quantum implementation. We develop Finite Imaginary-Time Evolution (FinITE), a finite-beta construction for diagonal Pauli-Z cost Hamiltonians arising from polynomial unconstrained binary optimization (PUBO) instances, including QUBO and HUBO cases. FinITE uses the linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) framework to implement a scaled imaginary-time propagator. The commuting Pauli-Z structure makes termwise block-encodings compose without product-formula error, and higher-order Pauli-Z terms are handled directly without quadratization. The structure yields an exact finite-beta identity between the LCU success probability and the ground-subspace fidelity. Combined with a gap-based fidelity lower bound, the identity yields a closed-form sufficient imaginary-time threshold beta-star for a chosen target fidelity. The threshold depends on estimates of the spectral gap and the initial ground-subspace overlap. Because the LCU success event is flagged by a known ancilla outcome, we integrate fixed-point amplitude amplification with an explicit query-complexity bound. Statevector simulations verify the identity on a five-vertex MaxCut (QUBO) and an eight-qubit cubic HUBO instance, and shot-based simulations on the MaxCut instance illustrate the predicted finite-beta threshold and amplification procedure.

AI.tldr: FinITE is a method for finite imaginary-time evolution using the LCU framework for efficient ground-state preparation in optimization problems.
AI.motivation: To address the limitations of nonunitary imaginary-time evolution in quantum implementations for optimizing binary problems.
AI.method: Finite Imaginary-Time Evolution (FinITE) applies a scaled imaginary-time propagator within the linear-combination-of-unitaries framework, utilizing commuting Pauli-Z structures for effective block-encodings without product-formula errors.
AI.result: The approach provides an exact relationship between LCU success probability and ground-subspace fidelity, establishing a sufficient imaginary-time threshold based on spectral gaps and overlaps.
AI.conclusion: Statevector and shot-based simulations validate the approach, confirming the effectiveness of FinITE in optimizing QUBO and HUBO instances.

title: Observation antibunching with classical light in a linear interferometer
summary: Understanding the boundary between classical and nonclassical phenomena is important for both fundamental researches in quantum optics and applications in quantum information. One of the most interesting research directions in this field is exploring nonclassical effects with classical light. In this paper, we will show that it is possible to observe antibunching with thermal light in a Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometer by treating single-photon detectors as photon-number-resolving detectors to perform photon-number projection measurements. Both temporal and spatial antibunching is observed via the correlation of two detectors detecting one and zero photon, respectively. By comparing the measured results of thermal and laser light, it is found that the observed antibunching arises from the combined effect of photon statistics of thermal light and photon-number projection measurement.The classical and nonclassical nature of the observed antibunching is analyzed. The results are helpful to understand the connection between classical and nonclassical correlation and may find applications in multiphoton interference and quantum imaging.

AI.tldr: This paper explores observing antibunching with thermal light in a Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometer, showing nonclassical effects with classical light.
AI.motivation: Understanding the distinction between classical and nonclassical phenomena is crucial for quantum optics and quantum information applications.
AI.method: The study employs single-photon detectors as photon-number-resolving detectors to conduct photon-number projection measurements, revealing antibunching in thermal light.
AI.result: Both temporal and spatial antibunching are observed, highlighting the influence of thermal light's photon statistics and measurement techniques.
AI.conclusion: The findings clarify classical and nonclassical correlations and suggest applications in multiphoton interference and quantum imaging.

title: Pauli equation in spaces of constant curvature and extended Nikiforov-Uvarov method
comment: 21 pages, no figures, to be published in Physics Letters A
summary: We apply the extended Nikiforov-Uvarov method to the non-relativistic limit of the Dirac equation with a Coulomb potential in spaces of constant curvature. In this case, the radial equation reduces to the Heun equation, and the extended Nikiforov-Uvarov method easily yields a quantization condition which leads to necessary condition under which the resulting Heun equation can have polynomial solutions. The energy spectrum implied by the quantization condition is virtually identical to the spectrum of a spinless particle obtained using the Schrödinger equation, except for the absence of the ``geometric potential", confirming the non-commutativity of the naive non-relativistic limit with the ``squaring" of the Dirac equation, first discovered on curved surfaces. However, the necessary conditions for the existence of polynomial solutions cannot be met, and this fact undermines the reliability of the results obtained. This circumstance forces us to conclude that the extended Nikiforov-Uvarov method has limited, if any, value when considering similar problems in quantum mechanics.

AI.tldr: The extended Nikiforov-Uvarov method applied to the Dirac equation in constant curvature spaces leads to a quantization condition, revealing challenges with polynomial solutions.
AI.motivation: To explore the quantization conditions arising from the non-relativistic limit of the Dirac equation and their implications for polynomial solutions in quantum mechanics.
AI.method: The study employs the extended Nikiforov-Uvarov method to analyze the radial equation, which simplifies to the Heun equation in a Coulomb potential context.
AI.result: The quantization condition derived is similar to that from the Schrödinger equation, lacking a 'geometric potential', but polynomial solution conditions are unmet.
AI.conclusion: The limited reliability of the extended Nikiforov-Uvarov method in similar quantum mechanics problems is confirmed, suggesting its restricted applicability.

title: Magnonic Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill states
summary: Bosonic quantum error correction encodes a logical qubit in an oscillator, avoiding the hardware overhead of large qubit arrays. Among such encodings, Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states are paticularly powerful because their phase-space grid structure protects against small displacement errors simultaneously in both conjugate quadratures. Here we provide the first protocol for preparing magnonic GKP states, which involves an ellipsoidal magnetic crystal effectively coupled to a superconducting qubit via a microwave cavity. The geometric anisotropy intrinsically squeezes the magnon mode, while the cavity-mediated qubit control realizes an effective conditional-displacement interaction. We show that two rounds of a conditional-displacement interaction and a qubit projective measurement yield three- and four-component magnonic GKP-like states. We also show how to realize single logical qubit gate operations, such as Pauli, Hadamard and phase gates, completing the logical Pauli basis of the approximate GKP code. Our results establish hybrid magnon-qubit systems as a promising platform for preparing bosonic code states, with applications in magnonic fault-tolerant quantum computation and quantum sensing.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a method for preparing magnonic Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states using an ellipsoidal magnetic crystal coupled to a superconducting qubit, enabling effective error correction in quantum systems without large qubit arrays.
AI.motivation: To exploit bosonic quantum error correction, specifically using GKP states, for more efficient logical qubit implementation and fault tolerance without the need for extensive hardware.
AI.method: The protocol involves coupling a magnetic crystal to a superconducting qubit via microwave cavity, utilizing geometric anisotropy and conditional-displacement interactions to create magnonic GKP-like states.
AI.result: Successfully achieve three- and four-component magnonic GKP-like states, and demonstrate logical qubit gate operations such as Pauli, Hadamard, and phase gates.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid magnon-qubit systems present a viable approach for preparing bosonic code states, paving the way for advancements in fault-tolerant quantum computation and quantum sensing.

title: Experimental detection of entanglement in multimode Gaussian states from high-order intensity correlation moments
summary: Quantum universal invariants of a Gaussian state's covariance matrix, which can be derived from intensity correlation moments, have been adopted to characterize the entanglement properties of Gaussian states via the positive partial transpose criterion, also known as the Peres-Horodecki separability criterion. Such intensity correlation moments enable the extraction of information about the covariance matrix without the need for a coherent local oscillator. Here, we experimentally detect the entanglement properties of multimode Gaussian states using high-order\,(up to sixth-order) intensity correlation moments. These multimode Gaussian states are prepared via spontaneous and cascaded parametric down-conversion pumped by a high-peak-energy pulsed laser. Their intensity correlation moments are measured using a pseudo-photon-number-resolving detector constructed through spatial multiplexing of 32 threshold superconducting nanowire single photon detectors. This method is successfully demonstrated for two-mode and three-mode Gaussian states and can be extended to $N$-mode Gaussian states with $N>3$.

AI.tldr: The paper discusses using intensity correlation moments of a Gaussian state's covariance matrix to assess entanglement properties, demonstrating this approach experimentally for multimode Gaussian states without a coherent local oscillator.
AI.motivation: To characterize the entanglement properties of Gaussian states and improve measurement methods for their covariance matrices.
AI.method: Experimental detection of entanglement in multimode Gaussian states using up to sixth-order intensity correlation moments, analyzed through a pseudo-photon-number-resolving detector system.
AI.result: Successful detection of entanglement in two-mode and three-mode Gaussian states, with potential extension to N-mode states.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method effectively characterizes the entanglement of multimode Gaussian states, enhancing measurement capabilities without the need for a local oscillator.

title: Observation of Universal Spectral Moments and the Dynamic Dispersive-to-Proliferative Transition
summary: In non-Hermitian systems, spectra can be maximally boundary-sensitive, yet bulk physics need not be. Here we experimentally show that spectral moments provide boundary-robust bulk observables in finite non-Hermitian lattices, even when the spectra undergo dramatic geometry-dependent reshaping due to the skin effect. Using a unified acoustic platform with full spectral reconstruction and time-domain access, we probe one-, two- and three-dimensional lattices and demonstrate that spectral moments remain nearly invariant across distinct boundary geometries while the corresponding complex spectra differ strongly. To connect the thermodynamic theorem to realistic finite systems, we develop a loop-counting theory that identifies the physical origin of finite-size deviations in terms of missing boundary loops, quantitatively captures the corrections, and predicts a scaling law, which we verify experimentally. Beyond acoustic spectroscopy, we reveal a counterintuitive dynamical consequence of moment invariance: a dispersive-to-proliferative bulk transition governed by bulk moment structure rather than spectral boundary sensitivity. As a result, local bulk dynamics can remain stable (dispersive) even in a $\mathcal{PT}$-broken spectral regime, challenging the conventional expectation that $\mathcal{PT}$ breaking necessarily implies feedback-induced dynamical instability (proliferation) through exponentially amplifying spectral components. These results establish spectral moments as practical bulk descriptors for finite non-Hermitian matter and open a route to extracting and controlling intrinsic bulk behavior in realistic wave-based non-Hermitian devices.

AI.motivation: The study investigates the relationship between boundary-sensitive spectra and bulk physics in non-Hermitian systems, particularly under conditions of the skin effect, challenging conventional interpretations.
AI.method: Experiments on one-, two-, and three-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices using a unified acoustic platform with full spectral reconstruction and time-domain access. A loop-counting theory is developed to explain finite-size effects.
AI.result: Spectral moments are invariant across different boundary geometries, while complex spectra differ significantly. A scaling law relating to missing boundary loops is experimentally verified, showing stable local bulk dynamics even in a PT-broken regime.
AI.conclusion: Spectral moments can effectively characterize finite non-Hermitian systems, enabling better extraction and control of bulk behavior in practical applications.

title: Quantum Magnetometry with Orientation beyond Steady-State Limits in Cavity-Magnon Systems
summary: We present a transient quantum sensing framework for cavity-magnon systems that circumvents the inevitable loss of initial-state quantum properties plaguing conventional steady-state protocols. Explicitly incorporating finite-time dynamics and adopting an engineered steady state as the initial condition, we derive the exact transient noise spectrum. We show that residual initial quantum correlations alone can drastically enhance the short-time signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) beyond that achievable with unsqueezed steady-state schemes. Through analysis of the transient spectral density and joint measurements of orthogonal cavity quadratures, we realize crosstalk-free reconstruction of all three magnetic field components, enabling orientation of magnetic signals. In the long-time limit, our theory yields a closed-form stationary noise spectrum and uncovers a resonance condition $g_{am}=\sqrt{κ_aκ_m}/2$, where cavity field quantum noise is fully canceled without requiring strong coherent coupling. Away from this resonance, injected squeezing further suppresses cavity induced noise and broadens the detection bandwidth. Extending the framework to an array of $N$ yttrium iron garnet (YIG) spheres generates a collective bright mode, with magnon-probe noise scaling as $1/N$. Our results establish a unified route to scalable, high precision, multidimensional quantum magnetometry using cavity-magnon platforms.

AI.motivation: To address the limitations of conventional steady-state quantum sensing methods, particularly the loss of initial quantum properties and low signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) in magnetic signal detection.
AI.method: The authors derive the transient noise spectrum by considering finite-time dynamics and using an engineered steady state as the initial condition. They analyze the transient spectral density and perform joint measurements to reconstruct magnetic field components accurately.
AI.result: The findings show that initial quantum correlations significantly enhance the short-time SNR. The theory reveals a resonance condition that enables complete cancellation of cavity noise without strong coupling, with further noise suppression achievable via injected squeezing. Additionally, scaling the system with multiple YIG spheres improves detection noise characteristics.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a method for scalable and high-precision multidimensional quantum magnetometry in cavity-magnon systems, showcasing the potential for improved magnetic signal orientation and noise reduction.

title: Effective Noise Mitigation via Quantum Circuit Learning in Quantum Simulation of Integrable Spin Chains
summary: We propose a noise-mitigation quantum simulation strategy for near-term quantum devices based on Quantum Circuit Learning (QCL), which is in particular effective for integrable quantum spin chains. The method trains a shallow variational circuit to approximate a deeper time-evolution circuit by learning the conserved charges and only a small amount of dynamical information in the system. Under realistic noise models, the learned circuit maintains both conserved quantities and dynamical observables significantly closer to their true values than the noisy simulation of the original circuit. This demonstrates QCL as an effective, physics-informed error mitigation strategy, producing shorter, more robust circuits without exponential sampling overhead.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a noise-mitigation strategy using Quantum Circuit Learning to enhance simulations in near-term quantum devices, particularly for integrable quantum spin chains.
AI.motivation: The increasing noise in near-term quantum devices necessitates effective error mitigation strategies to ensure accurate simulations.
AI.method: The approach involves training a shallow variational circuit to mimic a deeper time-evolution circuit by utilizing conserved charges and limited dynamical information.
AI.result: The learned circuit outperforms the original noisy circuit, preserving conserved quantities and observables more effectively under realistic noise conditions.
AI.conclusion: QCL is validated as a robust, efficient method for error mitigation, enabling shorter circuits with no exponential sampling costs.

title: An Analytical Approach to Design Space Exploration for Cavity-Mediated Quantum State Transfer in Multi-core Architectures
summary: In multi-core quantum computing architectures, waveguide-mediated interconnects are essential for facilitating fast, high-fidelity quantum state transfer between qubits located in different chips. However, optimizing these systems typically relies on computationally expensive numerical simulations that offer limited physical insight. In this work, we derive exact analytical expressions for the state transfer dynamics of a two-qubit system coupled via a waveguide, modeled through a Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian and the Lindblad master equation. We apply the Monte Carlo wave-function method and obtain a closed-form solution for qubit occupation probabilities that accounts for both detuning and dissipative losses. Our analytical framework provides a significant computational speedup compared to standard numerical solvers, enabling large-scale parameter sweeps while maintaining high precision in both fidelity and latency predictions. Furthermore, the model reveals and explains systematic low-fidelity regions arising from destructive interference between internal oscillations and detuning-induced envelopes, which are phenomena that are difficult to characterize through numerical means alone. Finally, we propose a simplified latency model and an efficiency-based function to enable rapid identification of optimal operating points. This analytical approach provides a robust foundation for the design and optimization of interconnects in multi-core quantum processors.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an analytical framework for optimizing quantum state transfer between qubits in multi-core quantum computing via waveguide-mediated interconnects, offering significant computational speedup and insights into fidelity issues.
AI.motivation: To improve the efficiency of state transfer in multi-core quantum computing architectures without relying on computationally intensive numerical simulations.
AI.method: The authors derive analytical expressions using a Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian and the Lindblad master equation, applying the Monte Carlo wave-function method to obtain closed-form solutions for qubit probabilities.
AI.result: The framework allows for faster computations compared to numerical methods, facilitating large parameter sweeps while accurately predicting fidelity and latency. It also identifies low-fidelity regions caused by destructive interference.
AI.conclusion: The analytical approach enhances the design of waveguide interconnects in quantum processors, providing tools for rapid identification of optimal operating points.

title: Observation of attractor transitions in active magnon-polaritons under microwatt drives
summary: Magnon-polaritons provide a room-temperature platform for investigating nonlinear cavity quantum electrodynamics in the microwave domain, but experimentally observing controlled transitions among distinct nonlinear attractors remains challenging in conventional passive systems, where strong external driving is usually required. Here we report the observation of attractor transitions in an active magnon-polariton formed by a self-oscillating microwave cavity coupled to a yttrium iron garne (YIG) sphere. The feedback loop supplies an internal microwave drive, while Kerr frequency pulling and Suhl-mediated magnon-magnon scattering produce an enhanced effective nonlinearity. Stability analysis using experimentally calibrated parameters reveals a rich fixed-point (FP) landscape with multiple unstable-FP phases and a triple-point region. By tuning gain across these phases, we observe the first experimental evidence of explosive growth of bistability, followed by transitions to multifrequency limit cycles, comb-like/fractal spectra, and broadband chaotic dynamics at microwatt powers. Near a critical point, magnetic-field-triggered switching between nonlinear emission states produces spectral shifts up to 162 times the bare gyromagnetic response. By enabling low-power attractor transitions and attractor-switching-amplified spectral response, active magnon-polaritons open opportunities for nonlinear microwave signal generation, high-precision sensing, and neuromorphic computing.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first experimental observation of attractor transitions in active magnon-polaritons, showcasing enhanced nonlinearity and pivotal applications in microwave technology.
AI.motivation: To investigate controlled transitions among nonlinear attractors in passive systems, which have been challenging to observe experimentally.
AI.method: An active magnon-polariton was created using a self-oscillating microwave cavity coupled to a YIG sphere, with feedback loops providing an internal drive and enhancing nonlinearity through Kerr effects and magnon-magnon interactions.
AI.result: The study revealed a rich fixed-point landscape with multiple phases, evidencing explosive growth of bistability and dynamic transitions to limit cycles and chaotic dynamics at low power levels.
AI.conclusion: Active magnon-polaritons enable low-power nonlinear transitions and significant spectral shifts, paving the way for advancements in microwave signal generation, precision sensing, and neuromorphic computing.

title: Parametrically Driven iSWAP Gate Using a Capacitively Shunted Double-Transmon Coupler at the Zero-Flux Sweet Spot
summary: A double-transmon coupler (DTC) enables a fast, high-fidelity CZ gate between two highly detuned, fixed-frequency transmon qubits. Moreover, a recently proposed capacitively shunted DTC (CSDTC) realizes a small residual ZZ interaction over a wide flux-bias range around zero flux, eliminating the necessity of static flux biasing while maintaining high CZ-gate fidelity. However, CZ gates with the DTC and CSDTC require baseband flux pulses with large amplitudes, which are vulnerable to pulse distortion and decoherence due to large qubit-coupler hybridization. To address these issues, we experimentally demonstrate a parametrically driven iSWAP gate operated at zero flux bias between highly detuned, fixed-frequency transmon qubits coupled through a CSDTC. Using a simple flux-drive waveform without predistortion, we realize an average gate fidelity of 99.92(2)% at a total gate time of 112 ns. The observed high-fidelity performance is consistent with small qubit-coupler hybridization and small effective ZZ interaction during the gate. Our numerical simulations reproduce the experimentally observed iSWAP interaction rate and effective ZZ interaction, demonstrating the applicability of the theoretical model not only to spectral information but also to time-domain dynamics such as gate operations. These results boost further progress in the research of superconducting quantum computers.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the experimental demonstration of a high-fidelity iSWAP gate using a capacitively shunted double-transmon coupler (CSDTC) for detuned transmon qubits, achieving 99.92% fidelity without complex pulse distortion.
AI.motivation: Existing CZ gates using DTC and CSDTC face issues with large baseband flux pulses prone to distortion and decoherence. This paper aims to demonstrate a viable alternative using a parametrically driven iSWAP gate.
AI.method: An iSWAP gate is realized between transmon qubits coupled through a CSDTC, operating at zero flux bias using a simple flux-drive waveform, with experimental fidelity measurements compared to numerical simulations.
AI.result: The experiment achieved an average gate fidelity of 99.92(2)% with a total gate time of 112 ns, showing consistency with small hybridization and ZZ interaction.
AI.conclusion: The results validate the theoretical model for both spectral and time-domain dynamics and support advancements in superconducting quantum computing.

title: Timescales for Deep and Full Thermalization
summary: Isolated quantum systems typically approach thermal equilibrium as described by the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH). Going beyond this involves either higher order correlators (full thermalization) or the formation of state designs, i.e., the approach of moments of state ensembles after a projective measurement towards thermal equilibrium (deep thermalization). We compare these two extensions of ETH using extensive numerical studies within a paradigmatic model for chaotic many-body quantum dynamics. For this we find exponential relaxation for both extensions: For deep thermalization all moments relax with the same rate, which approximately equals the relaxation rate of the autocorrelation function captured by ETH. In contrast, higher order correlation functions in full thermalization approach equilibrium faster. This means that at higher orders full thermalization is faster than deep thermalization.

AI.tldr: This paper compares two extensions of the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH)—full thermalization and deep thermalization—using numerical studies of chaotic many-body quantum systems.
AI.motivation: To understand the dynamics of isolated quantum systems in approaching thermal equilibrium beyond the standard ETH framework.
AI.method: Numerical studies were conducted on a model for chaotic many-body quantum dynamics, analyzing the relaxation rates of various correlation functions.
AI.result: Both full thermalization and deep thermalization show exponential relaxation; however, higher-order correlation functions in full thermalization approach equilibrium faster than those in deep thermalization.
AI.conclusion: Full thermalization is faster than deep thermalization at higher orders, indicating different relaxation behaviors in quantum systems.

title: Explicit Quantum Search Algorithm for the Densest k-Subgraph Problem
summary: This paper addresses the problem of finding the densest $k$-vertex subgraph in an arbitrary graph. This problem is NP-hard and has important applications in social network analysis, fraud detection, recommendation systems, and bioinformatics. We propose two quantum approaches to solve this problem: reduction to Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) and using Grover's quantum search algorithm. For the latter approach, we present an explicit gate-based oracle circuit utilizing Dicke states and Quantum Fourier Transform for edge counting. Numerical simulations demonstrate a quadratic speedup over classical Brute-force search.

AI.tldr: The paper presents quantum algorithms for the NP-hard densest k-vertex subgraph problem, utilizing QUBO reduction and Grover's search for improved efficiency.
AI.motivation: The densest k-vertex subgraph problem has significant applications in various fields, making an efficient solution crucial.
AI.method: Two quantum approaches are proposed: mapping the problem to QUBO and employing Grover's algorithm with a gate-based oracle circuit for edge counting.
AI.result: Numerical simulations show a quadratic speedup in solving the densest k-vertex subgraph problem compared to classical brute-force methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantum methods provide a promising direction for efficiently tackling a well-known NP-hard problem.

title: High-Girth Regular Quantum LDPC Codes from Square-Base Hypergraph Products via CPM Lifts
comment: 21 pages, 4 figures; ancillary TeX file included
summary: We study square-base Calderbank--Shor--Steane (CSS) hypergraph-product codes as a finite-length class for regular high-girth quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) design. For base matrices of small column weight, we give checkable conditions for regularity, rank deficiency, and short-cycle exclusion, and we present explicit column-weight-three and column-weight-four examples with Tanner girth 6 and 8. We also analyze circulant permutation matrix (CPM) lifts of this class. Using the standard voltage-sum criterion, we identify orthogonality-forced Tanner 8-cycles and show that CPM lifting cannot raise the Tanner girth beyond 8 when these cycles are present. As a representative finite-length instance, a randomized CPM lift of the girth-8 base construction gives a $[[28800,62]]$ girth-8 $(3,6)$-regular CSS-LDPC code. Under degeneracy-aware belief-propagation decoding with optional ordered-statistics-decoding-lite post-processing, this code produced zero decoding failures in $2.993\times 10^8$ independent trials at depolarizing probability $p=0.1402$; the Wilson 95% upper confidence bound is $1.28\times 10^{-8}$.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates hypergraph-product codes for quantum LDPC, providing conditions for their properties, presenting specific examples, and analyzing their performance under a decoding method.
AI.motivation: The aim is to design effective high-girth quantum LDPC codes that maintain regularity and prevent short cycles, enhancing their performance in error correction.
AI.method: The study establishes checkable conditions for properties such as regularity and short-cycle exclusion in square-base CSS hypergraph-product codes. It presents examples with specified Tanner girths and analyzes circulant permutation matrix lifts.
AI.result: A girth-8 CSS-LDPC code is constructed, demonstrating zero decoding failures in extensive trials at a particular depolarizing probability, supporting the effectiveness of the proposed method.
AI.conclusion: The findings verify that the presented CSS-LDPC code achieves excellent performance, and limitations on Tanner girth due to certain cycles are identified, guiding future code designs.

title: Compressed Sensing for Efficient Fidelity Estimation of GHZ States
summary: Accurately characterizing multipartite entangled states is a critical challenge in quantum information processing. In this work, we focus on applying compressed sensing techniques to efficiently estimate the fidelity of Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states. By exploiting the inherent sparsity of these states, our compressed sensing protocol drastically reduces the measurement overhead traditionally required for state verification while maintaining high accuracy. To evaluate the practical performance of this approach, we test the protocol on GHZ states using both quantum simulators and Quantinuum's trapped-ion hardware. Furthermore, we implement error detection techniques during our hardware evaluations, demonstrating the robustness and viability of compressed sensing for fidelity estimation in noisy experimental environments.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a compressed sensing approach to efficiently estimate the fidelity of multipartite entangled GHZ states, significantly reducing measurement overhead while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: Characterizing multipartite entangled states is crucial in quantum information processing, but it typically involves high measurement costs.
AI.method: The authors apply compressed sensing techniques, leveraging the sparsity of GHZ states to reduce the measurement overhead required for fidelity estimation.
AI.result: Testing on quantum simulators and trapped-ion hardware shows that the protocol maintains high accuracy in fidelity estimation, even in noisy settings.
AI.conclusion: The study validates the effectiveness and robustness of compressed sensing for fidelity estimation, highlighting its potential for practical applications in quantum information.

title: Entanglement of multi-qubit quantum graph states and studies structural properties of tripartite graphs with quantum programming
summary: We propose a method for constructing multi-qubit entangled quantum states representing weighted tripartite graphs. An expression for the entanglement distance for multi-qubit states corresponding to arbitrary tripartite graph structures is obtained. The entanglement of a qubit with the rest of the system in a quantum graph state is determined by the weights of the edges in the closed neighborhood of the corresponding vertex and by its degree with respect to other sets. We also calculate quantum correlators in the general case of tripartite quantum graph states. We establish a relationship between these quantum properties and the structural properties of the corresponding tripartite graphs, including the number of non-overlapping neighbors, the number of common neighbors of the corresponding vertices, and the number of 4-cycles. As an illustrative example, we consider a tripartite graph forming a triangle and compute the entanglement distance using quantum simulations on the AerSimulator with noise models. The numerical results are consistent with the theoretical predictions. The obtained results demonstrate that quantum graph states provide an effective framework for studying structural properties of tripartite graphs. They open up the possibility of investigating such properties using quantum programming. It is worth highlighting that tripartite graphs have applications in solving practical problems such as resource allocation, scheduling, and database and hypergraph modeling.

AI.tldr: Proposes a method for constructing multi-qubit entangled states from weighted tripartite graphs, establishing a link between quantum properties and structural graph features.
AI.motivation: To provide a framework for analyzing the entanglement properties of tripartite graphs through multi-qubit quantum states.
AI.method: Derives an expression for entanglement distance in multi-qubit systems and calculates quantum correlators, linking them to graph structural features such as neighbors and cycles.
AI.result: Shows that quantum properties correlate with the structure of tripartite graphs, illustrated through a triangle example with numerical simulations validating the theoretical predictions.
AI.conclusion: Quantum graph states facilitate the exploration of structural properties in tripartite graphs, with practical applications in resource allocation and scheduling.

title: Towards High Performance Quantum Computing (HPQ): Parallelisation of the Hamiltonian Auto Decomposition Optimisation Framework (HADOF)
comment: 17 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables, submitted to IEEE QCE 2026 and waiting for acceptance
summary:
Practical applicability of quantum optimisation on near term devices is constrained by limited qubit counts and hardware noise, which restricts the scalability of quantum optimisation algorithms for combinatorial problems. The simulation of large quantum circuits is also difficult and constrained by memory requirement. The Hamiltonian Auto Decomposition Optimisation Framework (HADOF) addresses this by decomposing large QUBOs into smaller subproblems that can be solved iteratively on quantum or classical backends. This allows the scalability of quantum QUBO algorithms beyond device limits, as well as their simulation on classical devices. In this research, we extend the evaluation of HADOF by benchmarking on real IBM QPUs across sequential, single-QPU parallel, and multi-QPU parallel execution modes, advancing toward High Performance Quantum (HPQ) computing for combinatorial optimisation problems.
  Experimental results on IBM quantum hardware demonstrate up to 3-4x reduction in wall clock time when utilising four QPUs compared to sequential execution baseline, while maintaining comparable solution quality. Notably, even single QPU execution benefits from parallelised job orchestration and execution, yielding up to 3x speedup. Simulated results predict over 5x speed-up in parallel execution mode. We further validate the practical applicability of the approach on real world genome assembly instances, showing that both sequential and parallel HADOF variants achieve competitive accuracy while significantly improving time to solution. These results highlight the importance of parallelism at both the algorithmic and system levels, positioning HADOF as a viable pathway toward scalable quantum optimisation.

AI.tldr: HADOF enhances quantum optimisation scalability by decomposing large QUBOs for iterative solutions, showing significant speedup on IBM QPUs and competitive accuracy in genome assembly.
AI.motivation: Limited qubit counts and hardware noise on near-term quantum devices hinder the scalability of quantum optimisation algorithms.
AI.method: HADOF decomposes large QUBOs into smaller subproblems, enabling iterative solutions on both quantum and classical backends; it benchmarks across various execution modes on IBM QPUs.
AI.result: Experimental results show up to 3-4x speedup with four QPUs compared to sequential execution, while single QPU execution sees up to 3x improvement; simulations predict over 5x speedup in parallel mode.
AI.conclusion: The results underline the effectiveness of parallelism in HADOF, establishing it as a promising approach for scalable quantum optimisation.

title: Heisenberg-limited Hamiltonian learning without short-time control
summary: Characterizing quantum systems by learning their underlying Hamiltonians is a central task in quantum information science. While recent algorithmic advances have achieved near-optimal efficiency in this task, they critically rely on accessing arbitrarily short-time dynamics. This reliance poses severe experimental challenges due to finite control bandwidth and transient pulse errors. In this work, we demonstrate that Heisenberg-limited Hamiltonian learning can be achieved without short-time control. We introduce a framework in which every query to the unknown dynamics has duration at least a prescribed minimum time $T$, and show that this restriction does not preclude Heisenberg-limited scaling. The key ingredient is a method for emulating the continuous quantum control required by iterative learning algorithms using only such lower-bounded evolution times. This reduces the learning task to sparse pure-state tomography. Notably, for logarithmically sparse Hamiltonians, our algorithm achieves the information-theoretically optimal $1/\varepsilon$ scaling in total evolution time for any arbitrary constant minimum evolution time $T$. For many-body (polynomially sparse) systems, we uncover a rigorous quantitative tradeoff, showing that the minimum required evolution time can be significantly relaxed from the standard limit at a polynomial cost in total evolution time. Our results affirmatively resolve a prominent open problem in the field and reveal that high-bandwidth, ultra-short pulses are not fundamentally necessary for optimal quantum learning.

AI.tldr: This study demonstrates Heisenberg-limited Hamiltonian learning without relying on short-time control, introducing a framework that permits a minimum query duration while maintaining efficiency in learning outcomes.
AI.motivation: To address the limitations posed by finite control bandwidth and transient pulse errors in current Hamiltonian learning techniques, which often require short-time dynamics.
AI.method: A framework is proposed where queries to the unknown dynamics have a minimum duration, utilizing continuous quantum control emulation to reduce the problem to sparse pure-state tomography.
AI.result: For logarithmically sparse Hamiltonians, the algorithm achieves optimal scaling in total evolution time for any constant minimum evolution time. For many-body systems, a tradeoff allows for significant relaxation of the minimum evolution time at a polynomial increase in total evolution time.
AI.conclusion: The findings resolve a critical issue in quantum learning, indicating that optimal quantum learning does not necessitate high-bandwidth, ultra-short pulses.

title: Wavelet-based multiresolution analysis of quantum fractals in confined dynamics
summary: Fractal structures naturally emerge in quantum systems whose initial states exhibit spatial discontinuities, a phenomenon first identified by Berry in the paradigmatic case of a particle confined in an infinite potential well. While previous analyses of quantum fractals have mainly relied on spectral decompositions and geometric scaling arguments, their quantitative characterization often depends on scale choices and truncation effects. Here we present a wavelet-based multiresolution framework that enables a direct and assumption-free quantification of quantum fractality. Fractal dimensions are extracted from the scale-dependent distribution of wavelet energies, without invoking prior power-law hypotheses. The method is applied to space and time quantum fractals arising in confined dynamics, as well as to dynamical curves generated by the associated quantum probability flux. These flux-driven trajectories provide a natural space--time parametrization of the underlying fractal structure and yield scaling properties fully consistent with Berry's predictions for space--time fractals. The resulting fractal dimensions are shown to be robust with respect to the choice of wavelet family, numerical cutoffs, and system parameters. Beyond validating earlier conjectures, the present framework offers a unified and computationally efficient tool for the multiscale analysis of quantum fractality in confined and interference-driven quantum dynamics. That is, it provides an operational, scale-adaptive criterion that unifies the characterization of space, time, and space--time quantum fractals within a single, hypothesis-free approach.

AI.tldr: A new wavelet-based framework is proposed for quantifying fractal structures in quantum systems without prior assumptions, enabling robust analysis of quantum fractality in various dynamics.
AI.motivation: To address limitations in previous analyses of quantum fractals related to scale choices and truncation effects.
AI.method: A wavelet-based multiresolution approach is developed to extract fractal dimensions directly from wavelet energy distributions, avoiding prior power-law assumptions.
AI.result: The method accurately characterizes space, time, and space-time quantum fractals, yielding consistent scaling properties with previous predictions and demonstrating robustness against parameter choices.
AI.conclusion: This framework provides a unified and efficient tool for analyzing quantum fractality across different confined and interference-driven dynamics.

title: Geometric complexity in thermodynamics
summary: The third law of thermodynamics forbids cooling a physical system to absolute zero in a finite number of operational steps. Although this unattainability principle has been quantified for specific state-to-state transitions, a universal, dynamics-independent bound for implementing a state-agnostic reset map remains elusive. In this work, we unveil the fundamental limits of physical map implementation by deriving a trade-off relation based on geometric complexity. By analyzing continuous paths of maps on a geometric manifold, we prove that the geometric complexity of any classical stochastic map or quantum channel is bounded from below by its execution error. As a consequence, we show that achieving zero error in a state-reset operation requires a divergent geometric complexity -- a unified measure that naturally incorporates disparate physical resources, including infinite time, energetic cost, or control bandwidth. This unattainability principle holds universally across both classical and quantum regimes, establishing a strict geometric limit on the physical realization of reset operations in thermodynamic control and quantum computation.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a fundamental trade-off between the geometric complexity of state-reset operations and execution error, indicating that achieving zero error incurs infinite complexity.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to address the lack of a universal bound for state-agnostic reset maps in thermodynamic control and quantum computation, despite known limits on temperature cooling.
AI.method: The authors derive a trade-off relation using geometric analysis of continuous maps on a manifold, linking geometric complexity with execution error for classical and quantum systems.
AI.result: The research proves that the geometric complexity of any stochastic map or quantum channel is inherently related to its execution error, revealing that zero-error resets demand infinite geometric complexity.
AI.conclusion: This study establishes a universal geometric limit on resetting operations, applicable to both classical and quantum frameworks, emphasizing the intricacies of thermodynamic control and computation.

title: Unentangled stoquastic Merlin-Arthur proof systems: the power of unentanglement without destructive interference
comment: 72 pages, 3 figures, 6 protocols, and 1 algorithm. Abstract shortened due to the arXiv length restriction
summary:
Stoquasticity, originating in sign-problem-free physical systems, gives rise to $\sf StoqMA$, introduced by Bravyi, Bessen, and Terhal (2006), a quantum-inspired intermediate class between $\sf MA$ and $\sf AM$. Unentanglement similarly gives rise to ${\sf QMA}(2)$, introduced by Kobayashi, Matsumoto, and Yamakami (CJTCS 2009), which generalizes $\sf QMA$ to two unentangled proofs and still has only the trivial $\sf NEXP$ upper bound. In this work, we initiate a systematic study of the power of unentanglement without destructive interference via ${\sf StoqMA}(2)$, the class of unentangled stoquastic Merlin-Arthur proof systems. Although $\sf StoqMA$ is semi-quantum and may collapse to $\sf MA$, ${\sf StoqMA}(2)$ turns out to be surprisingly powerful. We establish the following results:
  - ${\sf NP} \subseteq {\sf StoqMA}(2)$ with $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$-qubit proofs and completeness error $2^{-{\rm polylog}(n)}$. Conversely, ${\sf StoqMA}(2) \subseteq {\sf EXP}$ via the Sum-of-Squares algorithm of Barak, Kelner, and Steurer (STOC 2014); with our lower bound, our refined analysis yields the optimality of this algorithm under ETH.
  - ${\sf StoqMA}(2)_1 \subseteq {\sf PSPACE}$, and the containment holds with completeness error $2^{-2^{{\rm poly}(n)}}$.
  - ${\sf PreciseStoqMA}(2)$, a variant of ${\sf StoqMA}(2)$ with exponentially small promise gap, cannot achieve perfect completeness unless ${\sf EXP}={\sf NEXP}$. In contrast, ${\sf PreciseStoqMA}$ achieves perfect completeness, since ${\sf PSPACE} \subseteq {\sf PreciseStoqMA}_1$.
  - When the completeness error is negligible, ${\sf StoqMA}(k) = {\sf StoqMA}(2)$ for $k\geq 2$.
  Our lower bounds are obtained by stoquastizing the short-proof ${\sf QMA}(2)$ protocols via distribution testing techniques. Our upper bounds for the nearly perfect completeness case are proved via our new rectangular closure testing framework.

AI.motivation: To systematically study the impact of unentanglement without destructive interference in quantifying computation via the newly defined class ${ f StoqMA}(2)$.
AI.method: Analysis of proof systems, establishing containment relations and lower/upper bounds through distribution testing and a new rectangular closure testing framework.
AI.result:
${ f NP} 
eq { f EXP}$; ${ f StoqMA}(2)$ contains NP with moderate qubit proofs, while also being contained in EXP and PSPACE under various circumstances.
AI.conclusion: ${ f StoqMA}(2)$ exhibits surprising computational strength, challenging prior assumptions, and has particular constraints preventing perfect completeness.

title: Adaptable Continuous Variable Quantum Network with Finite Size Security
summary: In recent years, continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) has become a promising paradigm for enabling secure communication among multiple end users sharing the same telecommunication backbone. CV-QKD with reverse reconciliation naturally enables scalability from conventional point-to-point links to quantum access networks based on passive quantum broadcasting channels. Here, we report an experimental demonstration on an active $1:4$ multi-user CV quantum network (QN) in the finite-size regime. With $1.25\cdot10^9$ coherent states exchanged on each $11\text{km}$ quantum channel, the highest performance for secret key generation totaling $1.9\cdot10^{-1}$ bits/channel use. Furthermore, we investigate adaptable CV-QN protocols that comprehensively allow network operation in various security and key rates requirements of individual users. The results establish the practical security of CV-QN compatible with existing telecommunication for broad deployment, and allowing additional degree of freedom for connected end users in existing infrastructures.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates an active multi-user CV quantum network capable of secure communication with high key generation rates over quantum channels.
AI.motivation: To enable secure communication among multiple users using CV-QKD in quantum access networks with existing telecommunications.
AI.method: The authors experimentally showcased a $1:4$ multi-user CV quantum network using $1.25	ext{ billion}$ coherent states over $11	ext{ km}$ channels, optimizing key generation rates.
AI.result: Achieved a secret key generation rate of $1.9	ext{ bits/channel use}$, demonstrating practical scalability and adaptability for user requirements.
AI.conclusion: The findings confirm the practicality and security of CV-QN, enhancing its deployment potential in current telecommunication infrastructures.

title: Learning quantum disentanglement scheduling from reduced states via modular hybrid policies
comment: 13 pages, 11 figures; Preliminary manuscript prepared for summer program applications
summary: Quantum control with restricted state access is central to near-term quantum devices, where full wave-function information is unavailable. We study this problem through multiqubit disentanglement scheduling from partial observations, where a controller receives only two-qubit reduced density matrices and selects which qubit pair to disentangle at each step. We introduce a modular hybrid quantum--classical policy framework consisting of classical preprocessing, a parameterized quantum circuit as a compact nonlinear latent block, and classical postprocessing for pair-selection probabilities. Benchmarking 4-, 5-, and 6-qubit tasks, we find that preprocessing is the dominant factor governing performance under reduced-state observations, while the quantum module provides a conditional compact representation whose utility depends on the input features and model budget. We further identify a performance--efficiency trade-off across policy families and find that increasing circuit width is generally more useful than increasing depth. These results provide practical design principles for hybrid policies in reduced-information quantum control.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses quantum control in near-term devices with limited state information, focusing on disentangling qubits from partial observations using a hybrid quantum-classical framework.
AI.motivation: Understanding quantum control with limited access to wave-function information is critical for practical quantum computing applications.
AI.method: A hybrid quantum-classical policy framework integrates classical preprocessing, a parameterized quantum circuit for representing quantum states, and classical postprocessing for pair-selection of qubits for disentanglement.
AI.result: Benchmarking shows that classical preprocessing dominates performance, while the quantum module's effectiveness relies on the input features and model complexity. A trade-off in efficiency based on policy families is also identified, with circuit width being more beneficial than depth.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish guidelines for designing effective hybrid policies in scenarios of limited quantum state information.

title: Branch-Resolved Characterization of Feed-Forward Error in Dynamic Teleportation via Classical Choi Shadows
summary: Mid-circuit measurement and classical feed-forward are essential primitives for dynamic-circuit teleportation on superconducting quantum processors. However, the error associated with measurement-conditioned corrective operations remains poorly understood when evaluated with respect to individual measurement branches. In this paper, we present a framework for characterizing feed-forward error in dynamic circuit teleportation without losing valuable information related to its behavior across separate branches. We analyze three approaches to applying measurement-conditioned corrections: (i) physical application, (ii) post-processing adjustments, and (iii) a mitigated physical application which utilizes Bit-Flip Averaging (BFA)-based Probabilistic Readout Error Mitigation (PROM). We experimentally reconstruct branch Choi operators via an entangled reference qubit, and validate our physical-application and post-processing Choi-shadow estimators against full tomography of the branch Choi operators. We perform experiments on two physical qubit layouts which differ greatly in mid-circuit measurement readout error, and observe a reversal in the relative order in branch qualities obtained from the post-processing and PROM mitigation strategies. In one physical layout with higher measurement readout error, the operational feed-forward penalty is relatively modest (approximately 0.02-0.03) and PROM produces higher branch qualities than post-processing for every branch. In a separate layout with lower readout error, the operational feed-forward penalty increases to roughly 0.07, and post-processing exceeds PROM for all branch qualities. Our characterization framework can reveal branch-specific error structure and mitigation behavior that state-of-the-art outcome-averaged analyses fail to expose.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a framework to analyze feed-forward error in dynamic circuit teleportation, specifically addressing differences in error correction methods across measurement branches in superconducting quantum processors.
AI.motivation: To understand the measurement-conditioned correction errors in dynamic teleportation circuits, especially how these errors vary with different measurement branches.
AI.method: The authors analyze three error correction approaches: physical application, post-processing adjustments, and a mitigated application using BFA-based PROM, by reconstructing branch Choi operators experimentally.
AI.result: Experimental results show distinct behaviors of error mitigation strategies across two qubit layouts with differing readout errors, revealing that PROM outperforms post-processing in higher error environments, while the opposite is true in lower error setups.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers insights into branch-specific error structures, providing deeper understanding than traditional outcome-averaged analyses.

title: A No-Cloning Trade-off Between Black Hole No-Hair and Horizon Smoothness
comment: 5+10 Pages. To be submitted to a Journal soon
summary: The black hole no-hair theorem is traditionally derived from the uniqueness theorems of general relativity. We show that a quantitative form follows from unitarity together with the standard semiclassical assumptions of horizon causality and interior accessibility. For a semiclassical black hole, we prove that the trace distance between exterior states corresponding to two same-charge infalling states is bounded by $2\sqrt{2\varepsilon}$, where $\varepsilon$ quantifies the diamond norm departure of the interior channel from a perfect isometry which is a quantitative measure of horizon-smoothness violation that upper-bounds $1 - F_I$, where $F_I$ is the interior fidelity capturing how faithfully the infalling state is retained. Inverting this relation yields a trade-off inequality, $\varepsilon \geq D_{\max}^2/8$, between the maximum exterior distinguishability $D_{\max}$ and the degree of horizon smoothness. This establishes that observable exterior quantum hair is quantitatively incompatible with exact horizon smoothness under unitary evolution: any model predicting nonzero exterior hair must violate the equivalence principle at the horizon by a quantifiable amount. Pre-existing entanglement with the infalling system is the only channel for quantum hair compatible with both unitarity and horizon smoothness.

AI.tldr: The study demonstrates a quantitative relationship between exterior states of black holes and horizon smoothness, showing that observable exterior quantum hair is incompatible with true horizon smoothness under unitarity.
AI.motivation: To explore the implications of the black hole no-hair theorem using principles of unitarity and semiclassical assumptions, challenging traditional uniqueness arguments in general relativity.
AI.method: The authors employ a mathematical framework involving trace distance and diamond norms to examine the relationship between infalling states, their exterior representations, and the concept of horizon smoothness.
AI.result: They establish a bound on the distinguishability of exterior quantum states tied to infalling states, revealing a trade-off between exterior distinguishability and horizon smoothness, suggesting that nonzero exterior hair necessitates a violation of the equivalence principle.
AI.conclusion: Observable quantum hair cannot exist without compromising the smoothness of the event horizon, indicating that any model that suggests otherwise would breach fundamental principles in black hole physics.

title: Source-independent quantum key distribution without pre-sending entanglement
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables, accepted by Opt. Lett
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) theoretically offers information-theoretic security. The prevailing approach is the prepare-and-measure BB84 protocol, which implements QKD using conventional laser rather than single-photon source via the decoy-state method. However, side-channel attacks targeting sources severely threaten system security. Despite extensive efforts, including fully passive scheme, this vulnerability persists even with perfect single-photon source. Here, we propose a source-independent (SI) QKD protocol that resolves all known and unknown source-side attacks without pre-sending entanglement source. Aligning with advances in quantum light sources, our protocol simultaneously doubles the transmission distance while remaining robustness against imperfection of source. Theoretical analysis shows that non-classical light source provides practical security advantages unattainable with conventional laser.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a source-independent quantum key distribution (SI-QKD) protocol, addressing vulnerabilities to side-channel attacks and enhancing security and transmission distance compared to conventional methods.
AI.motivation: To overcome vulnerabilities from side-channel attacks targeting current QKD implementations and improve transmission distance and security.
AI.method: A source-independent QKD protocol that utilizes non-classical light sources and eliminates the need for pre-sending entanglement sources.
AI.result: The proposed SI-QKD protocol resolves security issues related to all known and unknown source-side attacks and doubles the transmission distance while maintaining robustness against source imperfections.
AI.conclusion: The theoretical analysis demonstrates that non-classical light sources significantly enhance security in QKD, beyond what is achievable with conventional laser systems.

title: Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Solutions for Transport under 3D Spatially Varying Advection on Trapped Ion Hardware
summary: The Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Method (QLBM) has emerged as one of the most promising quantum computing approaches for the numerical simulation of problems in computational fluid dynamics (CFD). The dynamics is formulated in terms of mesoscopic particle distribution functions governed by a discrete Boltzmann transport equation, comprising local streaming and collision operations. In this work, the resulting macroscopic behavior corresponds to the advection-diffusion equation, which we adopt as a canonical model problem for transport phenomena. Building upon recent progress in QLBM implementations, we advance towards more realistic problem settings that better reflect conventional CFD requirements. We address, for the first time, transport under the action of non uniform velocity fields on quantum hardware. We implement our demonstration using IonQ's trapped-ion systems including Forte generation systems and a 64-qubit Barium development system similar to the forthcoming IonQ Tempo line. We identify the density readout and subsequent reloading of the fluid density as a potential bottleneck of the current algorithm and discuss several approaches to mitigate this bottleneck. We identify the use of MPS shadow tomography as a promising method to efficiently scale the readout to large system with complex density distributions. Lastly, we introduce and simulate a novel method to implement wall boundaries for advection-diffusion in QLBM, and discuss the prospects of scaling to higher-complexity problems.

AI.tldr: This paper explores advancements in the Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Method (QLBM) for computational fluid dynamics, focusing on realistic transport problems and the challenges of quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: To enhance the applicability of QLBM in computational fluid dynamics by simulating realistic scenarios that reflect conventional CFD requirements.
AI.method: The QLBM is applied under non-uniform velocity fields using trapped-ion quantum systems, specifically implementing density readout and MPS shadow tomography to address bottlenecks in the algorithm.
AI.result: The study demonstrates QLBM capabilities in complex transport scenarios, identifies readout challenges, and evaluates methods to improve scalability in simulating fluid dynamics with wall boundaries.
AI.conclusion: The findings indicate significant potential for QLBM to tackle more complex problems in CFD, paving the way for future advancements in quantum simulations.

title: Nodal algebraic curves and entropy diagnostics in degenerate two-dimensional harmonic-oscillator shells
summary: Degenerate quantum eigenspaces can support substantial changes in nodal geometry at fixed energy. We show that, for the two-dimensional isotropic harmonic oscillator, this restructuring is organized by the Hermite-constrained algebraic curve $P_N(x,y)=0$ appearing in every real shell state, $ψ_N=e^{-αr^2/2}P_N(x,y)$. Finite singularities, $P_N=\nabla P_N=0$, and projective degeneracies of the leading homogeneous part identify the strata where topology-changing events can occur. We combine these criteria with entropy diagnostics: the nodal-domain entropy $S_{\mathrm{dom}}$, Cartesian mutual information $I(x;y)$, and the entropic uncertainty sum $S_r+S_p$. The first three shells reveal a hierarchy: $N=1$ only rotates a nodal line; $N=2$ has a conic transition at $b^2=2ac$, sharply detected by $S_{\mathrm{dom}}$ but not by global entropies; and $N=3$ supports cubic close-branch regimes organized by the projective discriminant, with enhanced responses in $S_{\mathrm{dom}}$ and $I(x;y)$. Thus algebraic stratification, rather than spectral ordering, organizes nodal geometry inside a degenerate eigenspace, while entropy diagnostics quantify probability redistribution and correlation. The framework suggests experimentally reconstructible signatures for real-phase Hermite--Gaussian structured light and approximately isotropic trapped motional systems.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies how nodal geometry in degenerate quantum eigenspaces, specifically for the two-dimensional isotropic harmonic oscillator, can undergo significant changes, structured by algebraic curves and analyzed using entropy metrics.
AI.motivation: To explore how nodal geometry in the degenerate eigenspaces of quantum systems changes at fixed energy, focusing on the isotropic harmonic oscillator.
AI.method: The authors analyze the Hermite-constrained algebraic curve associated with the system and combine this with entropy diagnostics (nodal-domain entropy, Cartesian mutual information, and entropic uncertainty sums) to identify topology-changing events in nodal structures across different energy shells.
AI.result: The study finds a hierarchical structure in nodal changes: for $N=1$ a simple rotation, for $N=2$ a conic transition indicated by nodal-domain entropy, and for $N=3$ the emergence of cubic branches associated with projective discriminants, with various entropy metrics revealing differing sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: The organization of nodal geometry is determined by algebraic structures rather than energy levels, and the proposed entropy diagnostics provide insight into correlation and probability redistribution, with potential experimental applications in structured light and trapped systems.

title: Weak-to-Strong Measurement Transition with Thermal Instabilities
summary: Quantum measurement is physically realized through a finite dynamical interaction between a system and a measuring apparatus, giving rise to a continuous transition from weak to strong regimes. While this crossover is well understood under ideal conditions, the combined role of thermal instabilities and pre- and post-selection open dynamics has not been systematically addressed. Here, we develop a general framework to analyze the weak-to-strong measurement transition in the simultaneous presence of environmental decoherence and thermal noise. We model the probe as a thermal Gaussian state, explicitly incorporating temperature-dependent fluctuations in the measuring device, and include open-system evolution of the measured system prior to post-selection. By deriving the apparatus's final state, we show that the measurement statistics are modified in a nontrivial, highly sensitive manner by the temperature regime of the system's thermal instabilities, the probe's thermal properties, and the particular choice of pre- and post-selection. This approach allows us to characterize how thermal effects reshape the weak-value condition and influence the emergence of projective behavior across the full measurement crossover.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a framework for analyzing the transition from weak to strong quantum measurement under the influence of thermal noise and decoherence, highlighting how environmental factors affect measurement statistics.
AI.motivation: To investigate the effects of thermal instabilities and open-system dynamics on quantum measurement, which have been overlooked in prior studies.
AI.method: A framework is created to analyze weak-to-strong measurement transitions by modeling the probe as a thermal Gaussian state that incorporates temperature fluctuations and open-system evolution before post-selection.
AI.result: The measurement statistics are significantly altered by the system's thermal instabilities, the probe's properties, and the pre/post-selection methods, revealing a sensitive dependence on these factors.
AI.conclusion: Thermal effects are crucial in understanding the weak-value condition and shaping projective behavior in quantum measurements across the full measurement crossover.

title: Reorganizing Quantum Measurement Records Improves Time-Series Prediction
summary: Near-term quantum computers are accessed through repeated circuit executions, which produce finite measurement records rather than exact deterministic outputs. In quantum reservoir computing, these records are converted to feature vectors for a classical readout. The standard expectation-value approach averages all shots from one labeled time step into a single feature vector. This reduces finite-shot noise, but it also gives the readout only one training example from many circuit executions. We introduce split-ensemble training: the same shots are split into groups, and each group average is used as a separate, partially denoised feature vector for the same target. The quantum circuit, task, and measurement budget remain unchanged. Across simulated forecasting benchmarks and real hardware experiments, this simple reorganization improves prediction when full averaging leaves the readout with too few training examples, with the strongest gains observed on hardware. Our results establish shot-record organization as a simple, broadly applicable algorithmic lever for improving near-term quantum learning without additional quantum hardware cost.

AI.tldr: Split-ensemble training enhances prediction accuracy in quantum reservoir computing by reorganizing measurement records from multiple circuit executions into separate averaged feature vectors.
AI.motivation: To improve the effectiveness of quantum reservoir computing with limited measurement records, which often produce noisy outputs.
AI.method: Introducing split-ensemble training, where measurement records are divided into groups, providing multiple partially denoised feature vectors instead of a single averaged output.
AI.result: This approach significantly boosts prediction accuracy in both simulated benchmarks and real hardware experiments when traditional averaging results in limited training examples.
AI.conclusion: Shot-record organization is an effective strategy to enhance near-term quantum learning, providing a cost-effective improvement without the need for more quantum hardware.

title: Defending Quantum Classifiers against Adversarial Perturbations through Quantum Autoencoders
summary: Machine learning models can learn from data samples to carry out various tasks efficiently. When data samples are adversarially manipulated, such as by insertion of carefully crafted noise, it can cause the model to make mistakes. Quantum machine learning models are also vulnerable to such adversarial attacks, especially in image classification using variational quantum classifiers. While there are promising defenses against these adversarial perturbations, such as training with adversarial samples, they face practical limitations. For example, they are not applicable in scenarios where training with adversarial samples is either not possible or can overfit the models on one type of attack. In this paper, we propose an adversarial training-free defense framework that utilizes a quantum autoencoder to purify the adversarial samples through reconstruction. Moreover, our defense framework provides a confidence metric to identify potentially adversarial samples that cannot be purified the quantum autoencoder. Extensive evaluation demonstrates that our defense framework can significantly outperform state-of-the-art in prediction accuracy (up to 68%) under adversarial attacks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a defense framework against adversarial attacks on quantum machine learning models using a quantum autoencoder, achieving significant improvements in accuracy.
AI.motivation: Quantum machine learning models, particularly in image classification, are vulnerable to adversarial attacks which compromise their performance and reliability.
AI.method: The proposed framework employs a quantum autoencoder for purifying adversarial samples through a reconstruction process, and includes a confidence metric to identify samples that cannot be purified.
AI.result: The framework outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to a 68% improvement in prediction accuracy under adversarial conditions.
AI.conclusion: This adversarial training-free defense framework offers a viable solution to enhance the resilience of quantum machine learning models against adversarial attacks.
